attribution.title: Marble Skill Taxonomy (v1)
attribution.standards: Curriculum standards referenced by the taxonomy have their own upstream licences (see PROVENANCE.md in that repository).
attribution.note: This is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Ages are approximate and the taxonomy is not written for learners with additional needs. Treat prerequisite links as a starting point and use professional judgement.

subject: Geography

topics.ds: Record locations on pictorial maps or simple models of familiar places (classroom, playground, home), placing pictures or objects in the right positions
e: Place picture markers for the sandpit, the office and their classroom on a pictorial map of the school
Build a simple model of the classroom with blocks and put a toy where their table is
Use position words to describe where a picture is on the map (e.g. 'the swings are next to the gate')
topics.p: Could {{name}} put stickers in the right places on a simple picture map of your street, home or their school — and tell you where things are using words like 'next to' or 'behind'?

topics.ds: Locate positions on a two-dimensional representation (simple map or plan) of a familiar space such as the classroom or playground, and move positions by following directions and pathways
e: Point to the teacher's desk and the door on a plan of the classroom
Follow 'forward 3 squares, turn left, forward 2 squares' on a playground plan and say where you end up
Draw a path on a school plan from the library to the canteen and describe it using left and right
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a simple drawing of the classroom or the backyard, can they find where things are on it and follow a path drawn on it?

topics.ds: Represent places at different geographical scales (local, regional and state, territory or national) on maps, and describe how people and places are interconnected across those scales (e.g. through food, jobs, services and transport)
e: Locate their suburb or town, its region and their state or territory on a set of maps at different scales
Label the state or territory capital and one regional centre on a map of their state or territory
Trace an interconnection across scales (e.g. milk from a regional dairy farm to a local shop, or travelling to a city hospital) and draw it as a flow map
topics.p: Looking at a map with {{name}}, can they find your suburb or town, your region and your state — and explain how things like food travel from farms to your local shop?

topics.ds: Locate the countries and regions neighbouring their own country on maps and globes and describe their direction and relative distance (e.g. Australia's neighbours New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, Timor-Leste and the Pacific Islands)
e: Locate their own country's neighbouring countries and regions on a world map or globe (e.g. for Australia: New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, Timor-Leste and the Pacific Islands)
Describe the direction of each neighbour from their own country using compass points (e.g. 'Papua New Guinea is north of Australia')
Use a map scale or distance tool to compare which neighbouring country is closest
topics.p: Looking at a world map or globe, can {{name}} find the countries closest to ours — and say which direction each one is?

topics.ds: Interpret and create two-dimensional representations (maps and plans) of familiar environments with a key and labels, locating key landmarks and objects relative to each other
e: Draw a labelled map of the classroom from above with a key for desks, door and windows
Use a school map to describe where the library is relative to the hall and the oval
Mark and label three landmarks on a local park map and describe a route between them
topics.p: Can {{name}} draw a simple map of their bedroom or the local park from above, with a key — and use it to explain where things are compared with each other?

topics.ds: Create and interpret grid reference systems that name cells or regions (e.g. B3), using grid references and directions (left/right, north/south/east/west) to locate and describe positions and pathways
e: Name the grid square that contains the playground on a map as C4
Describe a path from A1 to D3 using grid references and compass directions
Draw a 5 x 5 grid over a park plan, label rows and columns, and list the grid references of three features
topics.p: If {{name}} has a map with a grid of letters and numbers, can they find the square C4 and describe how to get from one square to another using directions?

topics.ds: Recognise that the school is on the Country/Place of a particular First Nations Australian people, name that people using information the school has confirmed, and explain in simple terms why Country/Place is important to First Nations Australians
e: Name the First Nations Australian people on whose Country/Place the school stands, using information the school has confirmed (e.g. from its Acknowledgement of Country)
Join in an Acknowledgement of Country and explain that it shows respect for the Traditional Owners and Custodians
Explain that Country/Place is important to First Nations Australians because it is connected to their family, culture and identity, and that people care for it
topics.p: Does {{name}} know whose Country their school is on — and can they explain why an Acknowledgement of Country is said at assemblies?

topics.ds: Describe the features of familiar places they belong to (home, school, park, place of worship), explain why some places are special to them and others, and suggest how places can be looked after
e: Draw a familiar place they belong to and label two features (e.g. the swings, the big tree, the front door)
Explain why a place is special to them or their family (e.g. 'Grandpa's garden is where we have picnics')
Suggest one way to look after a special place (e.g. putting rubbish in the bin at the park)
topics.p: Can {{name}} draw a place that's special to them — like the park or Grandma's house — label what's there, and tell you why it's special and how to look after it?

topics.ds: Describe how places change (seasons, growth, new buildings, events) and how they can be cared for by different groups, including First Nations Australians caring for Country/Place, council workers, volunteers and students
e: Compare an old and a recent photo of a local place and describe two changes
Describe how different groups care for places (e.g. council workers, Landcare volunteers, First Nations rangers caring for Country, students in a school garden)
Explain that First Nations Australians have cared for Country/Place for many thousands of years, using a story, picture book or local resource shared in class
topics.p: Does {{name}} notice how a local park or street has changed — and know that different people, including First Nations rangers, help look after places?

topics.ds: Explore how plants are grown for food, clothing and shelter — vegetables and grains for food, cotton for clothes, trees for timber — and grow a food plant themselves
e: Grow a food plant (e.g. lettuce, beans or herbs) from seed, caring for it with water, light and soil, and record its growth
Match plants to products (e.g. wheat → bread, cotton → T-shirt, pine trees → timber for houses)
Describe the steps farmers take to grow a crop (prepare the soil, plant, water, harvest)
topics.p: Has {{name}} grown something to eat — like herbs or beans — and do they know that their T-shirt came from a cotton plant and houses from trees?

topics.ds: Identify the natural, managed and constructed features of local places and describe their location
e: Sort photos of local features into natural (creek, hill), managed (park, farm, garden) and constructed (road, school, shops)
Locate local places on a simple map of the neighbourhood and describe where they are with position words (e.g. 'the park is next to the library')
Explain why a park is a managed feature (people plant and look after it) even though it contains natural plants
topics.p: On a walk around your neighbourhood, can {{name}} point out natural things like a creek, looked-after places like a park, and built things like roads and shops?

topics.ds: Explore how farm animals are raised for food, clothing and other products — how farmers feed, house and care for them — and what comes from them (milk, eggs, meat, wool, leather)
e: Describe how a farmer looks after an animal such as a chicken, cow or sheep (food, water, shelter, health checks)
Match animals to the products they provide (e.g. sheep → wool → jumper; cow → milk → cheese)
Order pictures of how wool gets from a sheep to a jumper (shearing, washing, spinning, knitting)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how wool gets from a sheep to their jumper, or how farmers look after the hens that lay your eggs?

topics.ds: Describe the interconnections of First Nations Australians to the local Country/Place, using information from local First Nations sources (e.g. local Land Council or Elders' resources, or books and websites the school has approved)
e: Name the First Nations people of the local area and, where the school has confirmed it, a local-language name for a place, river or animal
Describe from a local First Nations source how Country provides food, water and materials and how people care for it (e.g. seasonal knowledge)
Explain that the connections between First Nations Australians and Country/Place are spiritual and cultural as well as practical, and continue today
topics.p: Does {{name}} know which First Nations people's Country you live on, and something about how they are connected to the land, rivers and animals there?

topics.ds: Identify how contemporary Australia is represented as six states and two self-governing territories (the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory), locating each and its capital city, and recognise that Australia also has other territories
e: Label Australia's six states and its two self-governing territories, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory, with their capital cities on a map
Identify their own state or territory, name the states or territories that border it, and describe where one is using compass directions (e.g. 'Queensland is north of New South Wales')

Recognise that Australia also has other territories besides the ACT and the Northern Territory, such as Jervis Bay Territory and external territories like Norfolk Island and the Australian Antarctic Territory
topics.p: Can {{name}} find Australia's six states, the ACT and the Northern Territory and their capital cities on a map — and do they know Australia has some other, smaller territories too?

topics.ds: Compare the natural, managed and constructed features of places in their own country and in neighbouring or other countries (e.g. Australia and its neighbours)
e: Compare photos of an Australian place and a place in a neighbouring country (e.g. a Queensland coastal town and a village in Papua New Guinea) and list the natural, managed and constructed features of each
Record similarities and differences in a table or Venn diagram
Explain one reason for a difference (e.g. climate, landforms or how people use the land)
topics.p: Looking at photos of a town in Australia and one in a nearby country like Papua New Guinea or Indonesia, can {{name}} spot what's similar and what's different?

topics.ds: Describe the ways First Nations Australians in different parts of Australia (e.g. desert, rainforest, river, coastal and island peoples) are interconnected with Country/Place through culture, language, seasonal knowledge, stories and caring for Country
e: Compare how two First Nations groups from different environments (e.g. a desert people and the saltwater peoples of the Torres Strait) are connected with their Country/Place, using approved sources
Read a First Nations seasonal calendar for a region (e.g. from the Bureau of Meteorology's Indigenous Weather Knowledge pages) and explain how it links seasons, plants and animals
Explain that Country/Place shapes identity, language and responsibilities to care for it, giving an example from a source
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that First Nations peoples from the desert, rainforest and sea each have their own connections to Country — like seasonal calendars based on plants and animals?

topics.ds: Use an indicative map to recognise that Australia is made up of the many Countries/Places of First Nations Australians, which existed before colonisation and continue today, each with its own people and languages
e: Use an indicative map of First Nations Australia (e.g. the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia) to explain that there were hundreds of First Nations Countries/Places before colonisation, that they and people's connections to them continue today, and that the map shows general areas rather than exact, fixed boundaries
Find the general area of the Country/Place the school is on and name its people, using information the school has confirmed
Compare the indicative map with a map of states and territories and explain that they represent Australia in different ways, with boundaries that do not match
topics.p: Has {{name}} seen the map of First Nations Countries of Australia — and can they explain that these Countries existed long before the states and still continue today?

topics.ds: Describe the main ways of producing food and fibre — cropping, livestock grazing, horticulture (fruit and vegetables), aquaculture, forestry, and wool and cotton production — including First Nations peoples' food production and land and sea management
e: Sort products into the production system they come from (e.g. wheat → cropping, apples → horticulture, farmed salmon → aquaculture, wool → livestock)
Describe the main steps in producing one fibre (e.g. cotton: planting, irrigating, picking, ginning, spinning)
Describe one First Nations food production practice (e.g. stone fish traps or managing plants with fire) using a school-approved source
topics.p: At the supermarket, can {{name}} tell you how different foods were produced — grown as crops, in orchards, on grazing farms or in fish farms?

topics.ds: Describe the custodial responsibility First Nations Australians have for Country/Place and how it supports the sustainable use of resources (e.g. cultural burning, sustainable harvesting, seasonal knowledge and Indigenous ranger programs)
e: Explain what custodial responsibility for Country/Place means and give an example of how First Nations Australians practise it (e.g. cultural burning or harvesting only what is needed)
Describe the work of an Indigenous ranger group caring for land or sea Country, using a source
Explain how seasonal knowledge guides when and what is harvested so that plants and animals are not used up
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that First Nations Australians have responsibilities to care for Country — through things like cultural burning, ranger programs and knowing when to harvest?

topics.ds: Explain the importance of environments, including natural vegetation and water sources, to people and animals, comparing an environment in their own country (e.g. Australia) with one on another continent
e: Explain how a native vegetation type (e.g. eucalypt forest, mangroves or grasslands) provides food, shelter and other needs for animals and people
Describe the importance of an Australian water source (e.g. the Murray–Darling Basin, a billabong or the Great Artesian Basin) to farming, towns and wildlife
Compare the importance of an Australian environment with one on another continent (e.g. the Amazon rainforest) for people and animals
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why places like the Murray River or eucalypt forests are so important for animals, farms and towns in Australia?

topics.ds: Explain how and why food and fibre are produced in managed environments — greenhouses, irrigated fields, orchards, feedlots, aquaculture ponds and plantations — to control conditions, increase yield, protect crops and animals, and manage sustainability
e: Describe how a managed environment controls conditions (e.g. a greenhouse controls temperature and water; irrigation supplies water in dry areas)
Explain why producers manage environments (e.g. year-round supply, protection from pests and weather, higher yield)
Evaluate one sustainability impact of a managed environment (e.g. water use from irrigation, waste from aquaculture) and a way producers reduce it
topics.p: Could {{name}} explain why tomatoes are often grown in greenhouses or why farms in dry areas need irrigation — and one downside for the environment?

topics.ds: Describe how environments and communities are managed to reduce the impacts of natural hazards and severe weather events such as bushfires, floods, droughts and cyclones, and the consequences of these events (e.g. in Australia)
e: Explain how bushfire risk is managed (e.g. hazard reduction burns, cultural burning, fire danger ratings and bushfire plans) and the consequences of a major bushfire
Describe how a community manages flood or cyclone risk (e.g. levees, flood maps, cyclone-rated buildings after Cyclone Tracy in 1974)
Explain how farmers and communities manage drought (e.g. water storage and restrictions) and its consequences
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how Australians prepare for and manage bushfires, floods or droughts — like fire danger ratings, levees and water restrictions?

topics.ds: Describe the influence of people, including First Nations Australians and people in other countries, on the characteristics of a place
e: Explain how First Nations Australians shaped places through practices such as cultural burning and building fish or eel traps (e.g. Budj Bim in Victoria or the Brewarrina fish traps in New South Wales)
Describe how people in another country influence an Australian place (e.g. overseas demand for minerals creating mining towns, or migrant communities shaping a suburb's shops and food)
Compare how a place's characteristics changed through human influence, using two maps or photos
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that First Nations people shaped the land with practices like eel traps and burning — and that people overseas influence Australian places too, like mining towns?

topics.ds: Describe a country's interconnections with other countries through trade, migration, aid, tourism and culture (e.g. Australia's), and how these interconnections change people and places
e: Identify Australia's main trading partners and products (e.g. iron ore to China) using a data source
Describe an interconnection through aid, tourism or culture (e.g. Australian aid to Pacific neighbours, international students or sport)
Explain how one interconnection changes a place or people's lives in Australia or another country
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how our country is connected to other countries — through trade, tourists, students or aid — and how those connections change places and people's lives?

topics.ds: Describe the geographical diversity and location of places in the Asia region and its location in relation to their own country (e.g. Australia)
e: Locate countries of the Asia region (e.g. China, India, Japan, Indonesia and Vietnam) on a map and describe their direction and distance from Australia
Describe the diversity of environments in the Asia region (e.g. the Himalayas, monsoon rainforests, deserts, islands and megacities)
Compare a place in Asia with a place in Australia using climate data or photos
topics.p: Can {{name}} find countries like Indonesia, Japan and India on a map, say which direction they are from Australia, and describe how different their landscapes are?
